doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: State of jazz today and jazz education
summary: They say jazz is in flux with many good young players; seeing and hearing the music helps, as with Louis Armstrong in High Society.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: What do you think about the state of jazz today?
Well it’s too hard to answer. It’s too hard. I’m not too sure exactly how to answer that.
Only thing I relate is it’s in constant flux.
And a lot of great kids coming up too.

A lot of good musicianship, good soul feeling and everything. They’re really sincere, and not only in terms of dedicated to the profession, but their dedication shows because they’re reaching back in the history and getting the continuity you see. And in other words they’ve listened, like Papa Jo, pulled my coat, so in turn, I’ll pull my coat, so in turn, I’m pulling coats. So we have a relay stick. You pass the relay sticks. So out of that process, you could see some good coat pulling happening. And what has helped, is actually the increase in some aspect of recognizing jazz education, in the schools, and being exposed to it, now even at a much earlier age than ever before in the base, before ten, fifteen, twenty years ago. There’s a big increase.
And the things that you all are doing.
Well that’s a part of it yeah.
Because jazz has to be listened to, and if they can hear it from people who have done it, instead of imagining what’s going down, they can at least see us.

And the most important thing, if they can see and hear it simultaneously. So if it’s live it’s even greater, but if not, hey, a videotape or a movie, old movies and things like that, if it’s no more than that one little slot. Where like “High Society” we were talking about coming here, and I was watching it the other night, on the late T.V. movie, with Bing Crosby and Louis Armstrong, and Frank Sinatra. And it was a beautiful thing to see. Louis opened up the whole picture you know, and he said now the story began. And then we’d go through the whole thing, and then at the end, here they’re doing another number and he plays, and he takes his horn out and he says, “Now the story ends.” It was so beautiful.
No one else could have pulled that off.
Fantastic. Especially when he was so infectious, with his personality.
